title: Read-Write Lock
explain: A read-write lock has two modes over the same data. The write lock is exclusive and blocks everyone; the read lock is shared, so any number of readers can be in at once, but it blocks writers until they are all done. Use it when reads vastly outnumber writes, and be explicit about which side it favors.
model:
- **Write lock: blocks everyone.** Take it when you change the content.
- **Read lock: shared.** Many readers at once, but it **blocks writers until every reader leaves**. Take it when you must not see data changing under you: while you hold it, the content cannot change.

**Waiting policy.** The convention here is **writer-preferring**: once a writer is waiting, *new* readers are blocked, and the writer runs when the readers already inside finish. A reader-preferring lock lets a steady stream of readers starve the writer forever.

```
R1, R2 hold read lock -> W arrives, waits -> R3 arrives, queued behind W
R1, R2 release -> W runs alone -> W releases -> R3 runs
```

- **Worth it** when reads dominate and the read section is long enough that parallel readers pay.
- **Not worth it** for write-heavy data or tiny sections; a plain mutex is simpler and often faster.
- **Never upgrade** read to write while holding the read lock: the writer waits for all readers, including you.

details.a: Without it, new readers keep joining as long as any reader is inside, the reader count never reaches zero and the writer starves. Blocking new readers once a writer queues bounds the writer's wait; the cost is that new readers can be delayed.

details.q: A cache refresh job never gets the lock while readers arrive constantly. What is the likely cause?
details.a: A reader-preferring lock starving the writer. Switch to writer preference or a fair lock.

details.q: What happens if a thread holding a read lock asks for the write lock to upgrade?
details.a: It deadlocks, because the write lock needs zero readers and this thread is one of them. Release the read lock, take the write lock, then re-check what you read because it may have changed in between.

details.q: Four readers hold the lock for 10 ms each from t=0 and a writer arrives at t=1 ms. How long does the writer wait?
details.a: Until the last reader finishes at t=10 ms, so 9 ms. Readers arriving after t=1 ms queue behind the writer.

details.q: A shared lookup table is written on 50% of requests with microsecond critical sections. Read-write lock?
details.a: Probably not. Benefit comes from many readers overlapping with few writers; here readers rarely overlap, and the extra bookkeeping and writer handoffs cost more than they save.

details.q: How does this connect to contention in general?
details.a: A read-write lock is one cure for [contention](#/sd/f/lock-contention) on read-heavy data. The protocol itself is the same as [acquire / release](#/sd/f/acquire-release).

prompts.q: Explain read and write lock semantics and which side the lock favors and why.
points: Read lock means content cannot change
Writer preference blocks new readers when a writer waits

prompts.q: Walk through R1, R2, W, R3 arriving in that order on a writer-preferring lock.
points: R1 and R2 share the lock
W waits for both to release
R3 is queued behind W despite readers being inside

prompts.q: When would you not use a read-write lock?
points: Bookkeeping costs more than parallel readers save
